mission.title: Our Mission
mission.description: Jawafdehi is an open-source civic‑tech platform for Nepal built by Nepali to document allegations of corruption. Grounded in a Gen‑Z mandate for transparency and action, we aim to become the Nepali accountability system—holding corrupt politicians and others accountable through independent, evidence‑first, and citizen‑powered means.

caseArchive.title: CIAA Case Archive
caseArchive.detail: We index every case the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority files — including supporting documents, court orders, and legal filings, all in one place. Each record is structured so citizens, journalists, researchers, and volunteers can follow the full trail of a case: accused parties, alleged misconduct, locations, dates, official sources, and related documents.

plainLanguage.title: Plain-Language Summaries
plainLanguage.detail: Complex legal filings rewritten so any citizen can understand them — not just lawyers. Every summary is reviewed by human volunteers for factual accuracy before it is published. Summaries explain what happened, who is involved, what law or public duty is at issue, and where the case stands now.

aiResearch.title: AI Case Research
aiResearch.detail: Ask any question about a case or corruption trend in Nepali or English. Natural language queries against the full case archive will return instant, sourced answers. This research layer will help people compare cases, surface patterns across agencies or districts, and trace claims back to official documents.

cta.title: Know About a Case of Corruption?
cta.description: Help us hold public entities accountable. Report allegations of misconduct and contribute to transparency in governance.

recentCases.heading: Recently Documented Cases
recentCases.subtitle: Latest cases added to the archive

hero.heading: How a <1>corruption</1> case goes from discovery to the <3>public archive</3>

discovery.title: Discovery
discovery.description: Our data scraping team archives government documents, CIAA filings, court records, and CIB reports into digital text. The outreach team simultaneously works with investigative journalists, corruption watchdogs, and media organisations to surface cases not yet in the public record.

research.title: Research
research.description: Our research team investigates what constitutes corruption in each case, the role it plays in Nepali governance, and the effectiveness of existing anti-corruption frameworks. Every case is contextualised before it is written up.

compilation.title: Compilation
compilation.description: The compilation team structures each case: key allegations, timeline of events, entities involved, and all source documents. Cases are written in plain language so citizens — not just lawyers — can understand them.

aiDrafting.title: AI-Assisted Drafting
aiDrafting.description: AI helps our team process large volumes of legal documents faster — summarising filings, extracting key facts, and flagging inconsistencies. Every AI-generated output is reviewed and approved by a human volunteer before publication.

verification.title: Verification & Publication
verification.description: All cases are cross-referenced against at least two independent sources. Once approved, the case is published to the archive — permanently. Records are never altered without a visible audit trail and never deleted.

ongoingTracking.title: Ongoing Tracking
ongoingTracking.description: Published cases are actively monitored for developments: new court orders, verdicts, appeals, and entity responses. Updates are added to the existing case record so the full history is always visible.

sources.heading: Where Our Data Comes From
sources.description: We draw from official government sources, public records, media investigations, and independent civil society — and always trace every claim back to its origin.

ciaa.label: CIAA
ciaa.desc: Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority

hero.description: Corruption cases disappear from public consciousness. Officials retire, change portfolios, or simply wait for people to forget. We are building the infrastructure to make sure that never happens again.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.paragraph1: Jawafdehi is dedicated to promoting transparency and accountability in Nepal by documenting, verifying, and publishing corruption cases involving public entities. We empower Nepali citizens with verified information to drive systemic change and hold public officials accountable for their actions.
mission.paragraph2: Through rigorous investigation, documentation, and public disclosure, we aim to create a more transparent governance system where corruption is exposed, justice is served, and public trust is restored.

permanentRecord.title: A permanent public record
permanentRecord.body: Every CIAA case we document stays in the archive indefinitely. We do not delete records. Officials retire, governments change, and news cycles move on — but the record remains, permanently accessible to any Nepali citizen.

factsNotOpinions.title: Facts, not opinions
factsNotOpinions.body: We present original documents, legal timelines, and verified facts. We simplify complex legal language so citizens can understand what happened — but we never editorialize. Every claim on this platform is traceable to a primary source.

humanReview.title: Human review of every AI-generated summary
humanReview.body: We use AI to process and summarize large volumes of legal documents faster. But every case summary generated by AI is reviewed by a human volunteer for factual accuracy before it is published. Speed does not come at the cost of accuracy.

publicDomain.title: All data, free to reuse
publicDomain.body: The data we collect, clean, and structure is published openly for the public good — free to read, share, and build on for non-commercial purposes (journalism, research, education, advocacy) under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial (CC BY-NC) license, with credit to Jawafdehi. Corruption knowledge should not be locked away.

openSource.title: Open source technology
openSource.body: The software we build — from the case archive to the AI research tools — is open source and freely available. Any organization in any country can take our work and adapt it for their own accountability needs.

freeForever.title: Free, forever
freeForever.body: This platform will never charge for access. No subscriptions. No paywalls. No premium tiers. Public accountability infrastructure should be free to everyone who needs it.

volunteerPowered.title: Volunteer-powered, community-owned
volunteerPowered.body: Jawafdehi is built entirely by Nepali volunteers. We are not funded by government, political parties, or commercial interests. Our independence is structural — we have no institutional master to serve except the public.

techForCitizens.title: Technology in service of citizens
techForCitizens.body: Corruption-related records are scattered across dozens of government portals, court systems, and public databases — inaccessible to most citizens. We are building the technology to crowdsource and consolidate this knowledge into one permanent, publicly searchable archive. The goal is not a product. It is infrastructure.

cta.title: Volunteer with Jawafdehi
cta.description: Start by joining our Discord server or send us an email to introduce yourself and tell us which team interests you.

hero.description: Jawafdehi runs entirely on volunteer effort. Whether you are a technology enthusiast, a working professional, a legal expert, or a student, if you believe corruption should not be forgotten, there is a place for you here.

whoCanJoin.title: Who we're looking for
whoCanJoin.description: You don't need to be an expert. You need to care about Nepal and be willing to contribute your skills. Jawafdehi needs people who can help with technology, research, legal interpretation, data compilation, outreach, and translation.

globalCommunity.title: A worldwide network of Nepali professionals
globalCommunity.description: Our volunteers are based across Nepal and around the world — in the US, Thailand, India, and beyond. When you join Jawafdehi, you become part of a global community of Nepali professionals united by a single goal: making sure Nepal remembers.

technologyEnthusiasts.title: Technology Enthusiasts
technologyEnthusiasts.desc: Developers, data engineers, and AI practitioners who want to build civic infrastructure that matters. Frontend, backend, scraping, NLP — all skills are needed.

workingProfessionals.title: Working Professionals
workingProfessionals.desc: Accountants, analysts, policy professionals, and domain experts who can bring their field knowledge to understanding and verifying corruption cases.

legalProfessionals.title: Legal Professionals
legalProfessionals.desc: Lawyers, law students, and legal researchers who can help interpret CIAA filings, court orders, and legal timelines accurately for a public audience.

students.title: Students
students.desc: Students in law, public policy, computer science, journalism, or any field — this is real-world experience working on a problem that matters for Nepal.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.description: A few practical notes about supporting Jawafdehi. For receipts or donation questions, contact us directly.

items.q: Can I give monthly instead of once?
items.a: Yes. PayPal supports recurring gifts, so you can choose one-time or monthly support before confirming your donation.

items.q: Where exactly does the money go?
items.a: Donations fund hosting, document archiving, verification tooling, and keeping the archive free and open. Jawafdehi is volunteer-run and takes no profit.

For US taxpayers, yes. Jawafdehi Initiative Inc. (US EIN 42-3114954) is a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit, so gifts to it are tax-deductible to the extent allowed by law. Donations made through our Nepal entity are not deductible under US law. Email us if you need a receipt.

items.q: Can I support Jawafdehi without donating money?
items.a: Yes. You can help with research, translation, design, engineering, documentation, outreach, or reviewing public records. Email us and tell us how you would like to contribute.

hero.description: The components we build are open source and free to use. The full stack is public on GitHub — built by Nepali volunteers and made available to anyone who wants to build on top of it.

Jawafdehi runs entirely on volunteer effort from Nepali citizens across technology, research, journalism, and public policy. No corporate interests. No government funding. Just people who believe accountability matters.

meta.title: Where Nepal's corruption accountability leaks
meta.description: A quantitative read of CIAA corruption prosecutions at Nepal's Special Court — conviction rates, the charge types that stick, and where accountability is lost.

hero.title: Where Nepal's corruption accountability actually leaks
hero.lead: How many complaints become cases, how those cases resolve, and which charges the system convicts — drawn from court records ingested from Nepal's judiciary and the CIAA's own annual reports. Every figure links to the record behind it.
hero.snapshot: Snapshot as of {{bs}} BS, spanning 14 fiscal years of court records (FY2069/70–2082/83).
hero.methodologyLink: How we built and cross-checked these numbers →
hero.englishOnlyNotice: This report is currently available in English only.

funnel.heading: About 0.2% of complaints end in a full conviction
funnel.lead: In a single year the CIAA registered about 28,554 new complaints. Most were screened out at intake — only 947 (3.3%) went to a full investigation — and of those it prosecuted 137, roughly one in seven. Apply the measured full-conviction rate and only a few dozen end in a full conviction.
funnel.caption: Complaint, investigation and prosecution counts: CIAA 35th annual report (FY 2081/82), cross-checked against the court records. The steep drop is at intake screening, not the courtroom — most complaints never warrant a full investigation (many are outside the CIAA's jurisdiction or evidence-free); of those it does investigate, it prosecutes about 1 in 7. The conviction stage applies this archive's measured 45% full-conviction rate to the filed count.

stage.investigatedNote: only 3.3% go to a full investigation

funnel.workloadTitle: Why this starts at {{intake}} and not {{workload}}
funnel.workloadBody: You will more often see {{workload}} complaints quoted for this year, and that number is also the CIAA's own. It is the Commission's total workload: {{intake}} complaints newly registered during the year plus {{carried}} still open from previous years. Both appear in the same table of the 35th report. A funnel that starts at {{workload}} would count those {{carried}} a second time, having already counted them in an earlier year, so this one starts at new intake — which also makes the percentage at each stage smaller and more conservative than the headline version.

crossCheck.heading: Do the two records agree?
crossCheck.lead: The CIAA's annual reports and the Special Court's register are independent accounts of the same events — the Commission deciding to prosecute, and the court opening a docket. Across {{years}} fiscal years they agree to {{gap}}%: {{ciaa}} filings the CIAA published against {{register}} comparable cases in the register. Where they diverge it is almost entirely one offence — fake-credential cases account for {{fake}} of the {{net}} net difference, while every offence both sources label the same way matches exactly.
crossCheck.caseLevelLead: For the {{years}} years where the gap is widest we checked it case by case, matching the accused named in the reports' own filing tables against the accused named in the register. The direction of the divergence turns out to be the opposite of what a missing-records story would predict: every one of the {{listed}} cases the CIAA says it filed is in the register. What the register holds instead is {{surplus}} fake-credential cases that those years' own filing tables never list.
crossCheck.surplusTitle: Why {{n}} register cases are missing from the CIAA's own tables
crossCheck.surplusSub: Two of these reasons are documented rather than inferred. Five cases are a difference of principle about which year a filing belongs to: the CIAA attributes it to the year the Commission decided to prosecute, the court to the year the docket was registered — and all five appear in the previous year's report, with decision dates in Ashadh and filing dates that match the register's registration date to the day. Four more are absent from one year's report but described in the next report as prosecutions the CIAA filed at the Special Court and won: one CIAA document contradicting another.
crossCheck.caption: Filing counts from the CIAA's annual reports, cross-checked against the Special Court register. The register side removes {{excluded}} cases in streams the CIAA does not file — money laundering, petitions filed against the CIAA itself, and offences outside its jurisdiction — an exclusion that is marginally over-broad, since the FY2081/82 report shows the CIAA filed two money-laundering cases itself. Three limits travel with this: only {{years}} of the 14 years and one of the 13 offence families have been checked at case level; {{unexplained}} of the {{surplus}} surplus cases remain unexplained; and the reading that the annual report under-counts its own fake-credential filings is established for four specific cases and well supported for the rest, not proven for all.

outcomes.heading: Fewer than half of decided prosecutions end in a clean conviction
outcomes.lead: Of {{n}} decided cases with a clear verdict, {{conv}}% end in a full conviction, {{acq}}% in outright acquittal, and {{part}}% in partial conviction — so {{less}}% end in something less than a clean conviction.
outcomes.note: The CIAA reports a higher “success” rate because it counts partial convictions as successes; we keep full and partial separate and lead with the stricter number.
outcomes.grainTitle: What these numbers count, and what “partial” covers
outcomes.grainCases: These are cases, not people. The court records one verdict per case and publishes no outcome for each accused separately, so nothing here is a per-person conviction rate and none of it should be read as the share of individuals convicted. A single case may have one accused or a dozen.
outcomes.grainPartial: That is also why the middle category does two jobs at once. A partial verdict (आंशिक ठहर) covers a case where one accused was convicted on some charges and cleared of others, AND a case with several accused where some were convicted and others acquitted. The court's record does not distinguish the two, so neither can we. A partial verdict tells you the prosecution did not fail outright; it does not tell you how many people were convicted, or of what.
outcomes.grainFull: “Full conviction” (ठहर) is the strict reading: the charge was upheld against the case as the court framed it. We lead with it because it is the one category that cannot be read two ways — and we publish the including-partial rate ({{incl}}%) alongside it everywhere, so both readings are always available.

byCharge.heading: Conviction depends overwhelmingly on what was charged
byCharge.lead: Two charges carry the court. Fake-credential cases convict at {{fakePct}}% and supply {{fakeShare}}% of every full conviction. Bribery — the largest docket on the court, {{briberyDecided}} decided cases — convicts at {{briberyPct}}%, the second-highest rate of any charge and a shade above the court average, and supplies another {{briberyShare}}%. Between them that is four in five convictions. It is the rest of the docket that mostly fails: embezzlement, illicit enrichment and loss to government all convert in the low twenties or below, and illegal benefit sits at the bottom on {{benefitPct}}%.
byCharge.caption: Decided cases per charge type, split by outcome. Cited to the underlying charge sheets and court records.

justice.heading: Full-conviction rates run from 78% to 21% across the court's benches
justice.lead: The court records one verdict per case and no individual vote, so this is a property of the panels a justice sat on rather than of the justice: every panel member is credited with the panel's outcome, and a judge who dissented is credited with it too. Dot size is scaled to caseload. Sitting on the same court, hearing the same prosecutor, benches diverge more than threefold — but descriptively, not causally: some of that spread is the charge mix and the era a bench sat in, which the two sections above set out.

overTime.heading: The court convicts far less than it used to
overTime.lead: In the early years the Special Court fully convicted roughly {{early}}% of the corruption cases it decided; across FY2079/80–2082/83 that fell to about {{recent}}%. Acquittals now routinely outnumber full convictions.
overTime.rateSub: Share of decided cases by verdict fiscal year. Acquittals overtook full convictions around FY2078/79.
overTime.decompTitle: Is the decline real? Easy wins vs. core graft
overTime.decompSub: Documentary fake-credential cases — which convict at ~90% — fell from {{start}}% of the decided docket to as little as {{min}}%. Core financial graft, though, convicts in the same ~30% band throughout — so the headline decline is mostly that change of mix (the easy wins leaving), not the court convicting serious graft any less. The sharp dips (FY2078/79, FY2080/81) are acquittal spikes.
overTime.caption: Full-conviction rate by verdict fiscal year, case-grain, from Special Court records.

pace.heading: How long a prosecution takes, and when they arrive

volume.heading: What the court is actually asked to try
volume.trendTitle: Cases filed vs. decided, by year
volume.trendSub: Fiscal year. The filing peak (FY2076/77) precedes the decided peak (FY2080/81) by ~4 years.
volume.paceTitle: Time to verdict, and the backlog
volume.paceSub: By filing cohort. Cohorts through FY2079/80 took a median {{peak}} months at their slowest (FY{{peakYear}}); {{pending}} cases filed since are still awaiting a verdict.
volume.mixByYearTitle: How the charge mix shifted, by year
volume.mixByYearSub: Substantive prosecutions by fiscal filing year. Fake-credential cases (crimson) dominated the early docket — about 70% in FY2069/70 — then fell to single digits by FY2077/78–2079/80 (with a rebound in FY2080/81), while the newer illegal-benefit charge (absent before FY2078/79) and loss to government grew.
volume.monthTitle: When cases are filed, by Nepali month
volume.monthSub: Mean cases filed per Nepali month across FY2069/70–2082/83; error bars show ±1 standard deviation. Filings peak in Ashadh — the fiscal year-end — and trough in Kartik, the Dashain/Tihar festival month.
volume.monthCaption: Bars are the mean across 14 complete fiscal years (FY2069/70–2082/83); whiskers are ±1 standard deviation — how much each month swings from year to year. Registration date from Special Court records.

gaps.heading: Attrition concentrates at the CIAA stage — then goes dark

intake.title: Complaint intake & screening
intake.body: About 28,600 new complaints arrive a year and roughly 137 prosecutions come out the far end — near 0.5%. Most are screened out here: shelved, referred elsewhere, or closed for want of evidence or jurisdiction, and much of that is legitimate. But it happens with no public verdict on any individual complaint, which makes this both the largest drop in the pipeline and the least visible.

charging.title: Investigation & charging
charging.body: Of the complaints it fully investigates the CIAA prosecutes about 1 in 7, and what it charges shapes the outcome more than anything the court does. Two charges do almost all the work: fake credentials convict at {{fakePct}}% and bribery at {{briberyPct}}%, and between them they account for four in five convictions. Take those two out and the rest of the docket converts at {{rest}}%.

adjudication.title: Trial & verdict
adjudication.body: {{acq}}% of decided cases end in outright acquittal and {{less}}% in something short of a clean conviction, with more than a threefold spread across benches. Year to year the full-conviction rate has swung from about 86% to about 14%.

appeal.title: Appeal
appeal.body: The CIAA appeals many losses and defendants appeal convictions, but the record carries no decision data for those appeals. How often a Special Court verdict survives — or is overturned — cannot currently be measured from any public source.

recovery.title: Recovery & sanction
recovery.body: Billions of rupees in damages are demanded each year. No source tracks how much is ever recovered, or whether those convicted serve a meaningful sanction. The pipeline ends without anyone publishing what it produced.

gaps.lead: Follow one complaint from the day it is filed to the day someone is sanctioned for it. Five stages, two institutions — and the public record stops before the end.
gaps.caption: The dashed stages are not stages we failed to measure — they are stages no public source reports at all. That distinction matters: an unmeasured appeal outcome could be anything, and nobody is currently in a position to say.

appendix.heading: How this report was built and cross-checked
appendix.sourcesLead: Two independent public records, cross-checked against each other — and both browsable on Jawafdehi. Complaint, investigation and prosecution counts come from the CIAA's own annual reports; conviction outcomes come from our mirror of Nepal's Special Court and wider judiciary. Where the two overlap — the cases filed each year — they agree to 1.2%, and the section above sets out case by case where they do not. Every figure on this page links to the record behind it.
appendix.corpus: Corpus. Of ~12,600 Special Court records, most are procedural petitions. We isolate CIAA prosecutions as the Special Court's -CR- criminal register — 2,949 cases filed FY2069/70–2082/83 (the register is the definition; no plaintiff filter) — of which 2,795 are substantive corruption charges after removing money-laundering (a separate statute, 93 cases) and unclassified matters (61).
appendix.funnel: The funnel. Of 28,554 newly registered complaints in the year, only 947 (3.3%) went to a full investigation; most of the rest were screened out at intake — shelved or referred — much of it legitimate (outside the CIAA's jurisdiction, no supporting evidence, or duplicates). Of the complaints it fully investigated, the CIAA filed charges in 137 — about 1 in 7 (the CIAA reports this as 13% of its investigation decisions). So “0.5% of all complaints reach court” and “~1 in 7 of the complaints it investigates is prosecuted” are both true and measure different stages; the steep drop is concentrated at screening, not the courtroom.
appendix.outcomes: Outcomes. Verdicts are coded per hearing as convicted / acquitted / partial; each case is taken at its terminal deciding hearing. The conviction rate is over the 2,728 register cases carrying an unambiguous ठहर / आंशिक / सफाई disposition. That is a different set from the 2,740 whose case status reads फैसला (which the filed-vs-decided trend counts), and neither contains the other: 2,628 cases are in both, 112 are marked decided but carry no hearing with a recorded disposition, and 100 carry a disposition without the corresponding status.
appendix.derivedVerdicts: Where a verdict came from. Cases that reached the mirror without ever appearing on a published cause list carry no court-published disposition, so the only way to count them at all is to read the verdict out of the judgment text. {{n}} verdicts were recovered that way (37 conviction, 26 acquittal, 6 partial) and every one of them is EXCLUDED from every rate on this page — a rate that quietly mixed court-published and machine-read verdicts would misrepresent its own source. We report the number rather than filtering silently.
appendix.dates: Dates. Verdict dates are parsed from the case status text; filings from the registration date. Bikram Sambat dates throughout; by-year charts bin by fiscal year (Shrawan–Ashadh).
appendix.overTime: Over time. Yearly rates are grouped by verdict fiscal year; the sharp rise in acquittals from FY2078/79 is a genuine surge in the record, not a coding artifact. Time-to-verdict is measured by filing cohort: cohorts through FY2079/80 are essentially fully decided, but recent cohorts are still open, so their apparent speed reflects only the cases already resolved (survivorship) and is drawn as provisional.
appendix.justice: Per-justice. Attribution is bench-grain: every member of a panel is credited with the panel's outcome, so this describes the benches a justice sat on, not that justice's individual effect. It is descriptive, and small differences are noise.
appendix.discrepancy: Discrepancy with CIAA figures. The CIAA reports a ~53% “success” rate; that counts full + partial convictions together, whereas our full-conviction rate (45%) is cumulative and separates the two. Never compare the two without aligning definition and period. The filing counts are a separate question, measured rather than assumed — see the cross-check section above.
appendix.crossCheck: The cross-check. Matching the reports' per-case filing tables to the register is name matching, not a key lookup: the early high-divergence years print no case number at all, and a case number alone does not identify a court in any event — the same NNN-CR-NNNN format is used by the Special Court, the Supreme Court and the district courts, so a number lifted out of its column resolves to the wrong case. Names were matched after folding Devanagari spelling variants, and the residue was resolved by hand on the date: every pair we accepted matches the printed filing date to the register's registration date to the day. Three pairs were accepted this way and are flagged as such in the published data, so a reader who rejects them can re-derive the totals without them.
appendix.entity: Identity. Only ~7% of distinct defendants (607 of 8,321) are resolved to a canonical, cross-referenced identity, so office-level and repeat-offender cuts are deferred as low-confidence.
appendix.likhitPre: Reading the source PDFs. The CIAA reports are Nepali-language PDFs set in legacy Devanagari fonts that ordinary tools garble. We convert them to clean, checkable Markdown with
appendix.likhitPost: — Jawafdehi's open-source universal Nepali document-to-markdown converter — then verify every figure by eye against the original page.
appendix.limits: Limits. These are the records in the archive as of the snapshot date ({{bs}} BS); figures update as new records are mirrored. Appellate outcomes are largely absent, and amount-recovered is untracked anywhere.
appendix.grain: Grain. One verdict per case, because that is all the court publishes — there is no per-accused outcome in the record, so no figure on this page is a per-person rate. “Partial” therefore covers both a single accused convicted on some charges only and a multi-accused case split between conviction and acquittal; the two are indistinguishable in the source.

hero.title: Questions, answered plainly.
hero.description: Everything readers, contributors, reporters, accused entities, donors, and volunteers ask before using or supporting Jawafdehi.

questions.question: What is Jawafdehi?
questions.answer: Jawafdehi is an open-source civic-tech platform for Nepal, built by Nepali volunteers, that documents allegations of corruption. Grounded in a Gen-Z mandate for transparency and action, we aim to become Nepal's accountability system — holding corrupt politicians, individuals, and others accountable through independent, evidence-first, and citizen-powered means. We use AI to process government documents, track news sources, and generate comprehensive investigation reports, scaling the fight against corruption through technology. Free to use, open source, and **volunteer-led** — built by Nepali volunteers and a small paid team of intern lawyers and engineers who believe **accountability has no expiry**.

questions.question: What does "Jawafdehi" mean?
questions.answer: *Jawafdehi* (जवाफदेही) is Nepali for **accountability** — being answerable for one's actions. It's the principle the entire platform is built around.

questions.question: Who runs Jawafdehi? Is it affiliated with the government or a political party?
questions.answer:
No. Jawafdehi is **volunteer-led** — built and run by Nepali volunteers, supporting a small paid team of intern lawyers and engineers, in Nepal and across the diaspora — and is operated by two aligned, independently-governed nonprofit entities that share the name **Jawafdehi Initiative**:

- **Jawafdehi Initiative Inc.** — a Michigan (USA) nonprofit corporation, Michigan entity no. **900230142**, US EIN **42-3114954**, recognized by the US Internal Revenue Service as a **501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization**, organized exclusively for charitable, educational, and research purposes.
- **Jawafdehi Initiative** — a Profit Non-Distributing Company registered in Nepal under the Companies Act, 2006 (Nepal's legal form for a not-for-profit), registration no. **393949/82/83**, PAN **623632659**, registered with Nepal's Social Welfare Council (SWC reg. no. **59304**), incorporated June 2026, registered office in Biratnagar Metropolitan City Ward 5, Morang.

Our boards of directors:

- **Jawafdehi Initiative Inc. (US):** Bishwas Gautam, Nischal Dahal, Anish Karki.
- **Jawafdehi Initiative (Nepal):** Damodar Dahal (Chairperson), Niroj Aryal (Secretary), Medha Sharma, Rohan Raj Gautam, Shikshita Bhandari.

Our incorporation documents are public — the US Articles of Incorporation and IRS EIN letter for Jawafdehi Initiative Inc., and the Nepal certificate of incorporation for Jawafdehi Initiative. We accept **no funding from any government or political party**, and nothing that would compromise our editorial independence. We are not a government body, law firm, or legal authority.

questions.question: What kinds of cases does Jawafdehi cover?
questions.answer: Our primary focus today — and the core of our roadmap — is corruption cases filed by the **CIAA** (Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority): we index each with its supporting documents, court orders, and legal filings as a structured, plain-language record. We are **not CIAA-exclusive** — our longer-term goal is to also document major cases of national public interest that fall outside CIAA filings, such as the Ncell, Giribandhu, and Rabi Lamichhane cases. Each entry lets citizens, journalists, researchers, and volunteers follow the full trail of a case: the accused parties, the alleged misconduct, locations, dates, official sources, and related documents.

questions.question: Where does the information come from?
questions.answer: Today, most cases are built from **CIAA filings and the official documents, court orders, and legal records attached to them**. For the broader cases of national interest, we also draw on court records, the Attorney General's Office, official government documents, and credible media reporting. Everything is public and verifiable — we add plain-language summaries (human-reviewed) and link every fact back to its primary source, so you can check it yourself.

questions.question: What counts as "corruption"?
questions.answer:
Corruption is the **abuse of entrusted power for private gain** — a betrayal of public trust. The forms we track are:

- **Bribery** — offering, giving, receiving, or soliciting something of value to influence an official.
- **Embezzlement** — theft or misappropriation of funds placed in one's trust.
- **Nepotism & favoritism** — favoring relatives or friends regardless of merit, especially in hiring or contracts.
- **Conflict of interest** — personal interests improperly influencing professional duties.
- **Abuse of public resources** — misuse of public funds, assets, or authority for personal benefit.

sections.title: How it works & how we keep it accurate

questions.question: How do you verify a case before publishing?
questions.answer:
Every case undergoes a multi-stage review before publication:

1. **Source collection** — we gather government records, media reports, NGO investigations, public documents, and credible whistleblower accounts.
2. **Cross-verification** — multiple independent sources are required; claims must be corroborated through official documents, witness accounts, or verifiable evidence.
3. **Team review** — our moderation team reviews each case for accuracy, legal compliance, and ethical standards before approval.
4. **Continuous updates** — cases are monitored; updates, responses from accused entities, and investigation outcomes are added as they emerge.

Our standards require a **minimum of two independent, credible sources** per allegation; official documentation wherever possible; a clear distinction between verified facts, allegations, and ongoing investigations; a **right to respond for all accused entities**; and protection of sources and sensitive information.

questions.question: Do you use AI? Can I trust it?
questions.answer: Yes. We use AI — including Anthropic's Claude — to process and summarize large volumes of legal documents faster. But **every case summary generated by AI is reviewed by a human volunteer for factual accuracy before it is published.** Speed does not come at the cost of accuracy. Where we use Claude, submitted content is processed under Anthropic's commercial terms and is **not used to train their models**.

questions.question: What if information on the platform is inaccurate?
questions.answer: Despite our rigorous process, errors can occur. If you find inaccurate information, contact us through our feedback form with supporting evidence. We'll review and correct any verified inaccuracy promptly, and **all corrections are documented in the case's audit trail**.

questions.question: Can accused entities respond to allegations?
questions.answer: Yes — the **right to respond** is core to how we work. There's no self-serve submission portal; instead, an accused individual or organization should **contact the Jawafdehi team directly** at inquiry@jawafdehi.org. We first **verify identity through established, official channels** (for example, an official social-media account or a video call), and once verified, we publish the response **alongside** the original allegation so readers get the full context.

questions.question: How do I report a corruption case?
questions.answer:
Use the **"Report a case" form** on jawafdehi.org and include as much detail and supporting documentation as you can. You may submit **anonymously or with your identity**. Every submission is reviewed by our team before anything is published, and we may contact you for verification if you've left a way to reach you.

You can also reach us at **report@jawafdehi.org** or **WhatsApp +977 9768630501**.

If you'd prefer to go straight to the authorities, you can report corruption through official channels: the **CIAA** — hotline **107**, toll-free **1660-01-22233**, or **ujuri@ciaa.gov.np** — and **Transparency International Nepal** (transparency.org/en/report-corruption/nepal).

questions.question: What happens after I submit?
questions.answer: Your submission enters our verification queue. Our team reviews the information, corroborates it through multiple sources, and decides whether it meets our publication standards. **This typically takes 7–14 days, depending on case complexity.** If you provided contact details, we'll notify you of the outcome.

questions.question: If I report anonymously, is my identity protected?
questions.answer: Yes. We practice **minimal data collection**. Anonymous submissions don't store identifying information, you're never required to give a name or email, and access to submissions is limited to authorized personnel. We **never publish a source's identity without their informed consent**, and personal data like phone numbers and national ID numbers are never published. If you're concerned about safety, leave identifying details out of your submission and consider privacy tools such as the **Tor Browser** when using the platform.

questions.question: Can I reuse the information — for journalism, research, or advocacy?
questions.answer: Yes — for **non-commercial** use. Published case data is licensed under **Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 (CC BY-NC 4.0)**: you may read, share, and build on it for non-commercial purposes — journalism, research, education, advocacy — as long as you **credit Jawafdehi.org**. For **commercial** use, you'll need a separate license from us (which carries ethical-use terms) — write to inquiry@jawafdehi.org. We deliberately do **not** place the data in the public domain, so the archive stays the single authoritative, correctable source.

questions.question: Is it free? Will it ever have a paywall?
questions.answer: It's **free, forever** — no subscriptions, no paywalls, no premium tiers, no ads. Public accountability infrastructure should be free to everyone who needs it.

questions.question: Is the platform open source?
questions.answer: Yes — our core platforms are open source: the **Jawafdehi API**, our case **reviewers and graders**, **NES** (Nepal Entity Service), **NGM** (Nepal Governance Modernization), and **likhit**, our universal Markdown converter for Nepali documents. A few internal tools stay private, but we're strong believers in open source and in giving back to the community.

questions.question: What do you do with my data?
questions.answer: We practice **minimal data collection and maximum transparency**. All submissions are voluntary — you can report or send feedback anonymously, without a name or email. We minimize the data we collect, limit access to submissions to authorized personnel, and never sell, rent, or share personal information for commercial purposes. Full detail is in the Privacy Policy.

questions.question: How can I volunteer? Do I need to be an expert?
questions.answer: You don't need to be an expert — you need to care about Nepal and be willing to contribute your skills. We're looking for technologists, working professionals, legal minds, and students to help across our teams: data scraping, outreach, platform development, case compilation, and corruption research. You'll join a global community of Nepali volunteers in Nepal and across the diaspora (US, Thailand, India, and beyond). Email us to introduce yourself.

questions.question: How can I support Jawafdehi financially?
questions.answer: You can support us via **PayPal**, **international bank wire (SWIFT)**, or a **Nepal bank account**. Your contribution **primarily supports employment** — paying the people who research, verify, and maintain the archive — along with the hosting and tooling that keep it running and free to use. Jawafdehi takes no profit.

questions.question: Can I help without donating money?
questions.answer: Yes. You can contribute research, translation, design, engineering, documentation, outreach, or help reviewing public records. Email us and tell us how you'd like to contribute.

questions.question: How is Jawafdehi funded?
questions.answer: Jawafdehi is **volunteer-led and takes no profit**. It's funded by its volunteers and supporters, and by partnerships with **Nepali organizations and small Nepali businesses** that share our mission (for example, through donated infrastructure and services). We accept **no funding from any government or political party**, and nothing that would compromise our editorial independence.

questions.question: Are you a court or government authority? Can you prosecute?
questions.answer: No. Jawafdehi is an open-source documentation and public-awareness platform run by volunteers — **not** a government entity, judiciary body, or law firm, and not a legal authority. We don't prosecute, adjudicate, or give legal advice. Case information is based on publicly available records, may not reflect the most current legal status, and should not be treated as legal fact or used as the sole basis for any legal decision.
